entries.genesis 29:11: Jacob was overcome with joy and wept, then kissed Rachel. His long journey and the emotion of finding family brought him to tears.
entries.genesis 29:12: Jacob told Rachel he was her relative and Rebekah's son, and she ran to tell her father. The news would matter greatly to her family.
entries.genesis 29:13: When Laban heard about Jacob, he ran to meet him, embraced and kissed him, and brought him home, and Jacob told him everything. Laban welcomed his nephew warmly.
entries.genesis 29:14: Laban told Jacob they were truly close family, and Jacob stayed with him for a month. Family ties gave Jacob a place to stay, but the free stay would soon lead to a work arrangement.
entries.genesis 29:15: Laban asked Jacob whether he should work for nothing just because they were relatives, and asked what wages he wanted. It was fair to settle payment rather than let Jacob work without terms.
entries.genesis 29:16: Laban had two daughters: the older was named Leah and the younger was named Rachel. Knowing their names and order matters for what happens next.
entries.genesis 29:17: Leah's eyes were weak or dull, but Rachel was beautiful in face and figure. The text notes a contrast in appearance between the two sisters.
entries.genesis 29:18: Jacob loved Rachel and offered to work seven years for her, Laban's younger daughter. He was willing to pay a high price in labor for the woman he loved.
entries.genesis 29:19: Laban agreed it was better for Jacob to have her than a stranger, and told him to stay. Laban accepted the offer, though his motives were not entirely generous.
entries.genesis 29:20: Jacob worked seven years for Rachel, and because he loved her so much, the time felt short to him. Love can make hard work feel light.
entries.genesis 29:21: When the seven years were finished, Jacob asked Laban to give him his wife so they could be married. He expected the agreed deal to be honored.
entries.genesis 29:22: Laban gathered all the men of the place and held a wedding feast. It looked like a normal celebration, which made what followed a deception.
entries.genesis 29:23: That evening Laban brought his daughter Leah to Jacob, and Jacob slept with her, apparently not realizing it was not Rachel. Jacob was deceived in the dark.
entries.genesis 29:24: Laban gave his servant girl Zilpah to Leah to be her maid. This was a customary gift for a bride in that culture.
entries.genesis 29:25: In the morning Jacob saw it was Leah and angrily asked Laban what he had done and why he had tricked him after all his work for Rachel. Jacob had been cheated by his own relative.
entries.genesis 29:26: Laban excused himself by saying it was not their custom to marry off the younger daughter before the older. He used local custom to justify his deception.
entries.genesis 29:27: Laban told Jacob to finish the week of wedding celebration and then he would give him Rachel too, in exchange for another seven years of work. The trick came with a costly condition.
entries.genesis 29:28: Jacob agreed, and after the week was over, Laban gave him Rachel as his wife. Jacob now had both sisters as wives, which would bring trouble later.
entries.genesis 29:29: Laban gave his servant girl Bilhah to Rachel to be her maid. Like Zilpah, she was a wedding gift to the bride.
entries.genesis 29:30: Jacob married Rachel and loved her more than Leah, and he worked another seven years for Laban. The favoritism in this household would cause deep pain.
entries.genesis 29:31: The Lord saw that Leah was unloved and gave her a child, while Rachel had none. God notices people who are overlooked and acts on their behalf.
entries.genesis 29:32: Leah had a son and named him Reuben, saying the Lord had seen her sorrow and hoping her husband would now love her. She longed for love and saw her child as God's answer.
entries.genesis 29:33: She had another son and named him Simeon, saying the Lord heard that she was unloved and gave her this son too. She kept bringing her hurt to God.
entries.genesis 29:34: She had a third son and named him Levi, saying now her husband would be joined to her because she had given him three sons. She still hoped the children would win her husband's affection.
entries.genesis 29:35: She had a fourth son and named him Judah, saying this time she would praise the Lord, and then she stopped having children for a while. Her focus shifted from her husband's love to thanking God.
entries.genesis 30:1: Rachel was deeply jealous of her sister Leah because she had no children, and she told Jacob she would rather die than stay childless. Her pain was real, but she aimed it at the wrong person.
entries.genesis 30:2: Jacob got angry and reminded Rachel that only God controls whether a woman has children. He was right that this was God's business, but his anger added hurt instead of comfort.
entries.genesis 30:3: Rachel offered her servant Bilhah to Jacob so she could have children through her, a common custom of that time. She was trying to solve her problem her own way.
entries.genesis 30:4: Rachel gave her servant Bilhah to Jacob as a wife, and he slept with her. This followed the custom Rachel proposed, though it created a complicated family.
entries.genesis 30:5: Bilhah became pregnant and had a son. The plan Rachel arranged produced the child she wanted.
entries.genesis 30:6: Rachel named the boy Dan, saying God had judged her case and listened to her. She saw the birth as God defending her side.
entries.genesis 30:7: Bilhah became pregnant again and had a second son for Rachel. The family kept growing through this arrangement.
entries.genesis 30:8: Rachel named the second boy Naphtali, describing her struggle with her sister as a fight she had won. She framed the births as a victory over Leah.
entries.genesis 30:9: When Leah stopped having children for a while, she gave her servant Zilpah to Jacob as a wife too. She copied the same approach her sister had used.
entries.genesis 30:10: Zilpah, Leah's servant, gave birth to a son. Leah's household grew through her servant.
entries.genesis 30:11: Leah named the boy Gad, expressing that things had gone well for her. She saw the birth as good fortune.
entries.genesis 30:12: Zilpah gave birth to a second son for Leah. The rivalry between the sisters kept producing more children.
entries.genesis 30:13: Leah named the boy Asher, saying she was happy and other women would call her blessed. She felt her joy was now visible to everyone.
entries.genesis 30:14: During harvest, Leah's son Reuben found some love-fruits in the field and brought them to his mother, and Rachel asked for some. These plants were thought to help with fertility, so the request mattered to both women.
entries.genesis 30:15: Leah accused Rachel of already taking her husband and now wanting her son's love-fruits too. Rachel traded Jacob's company that night for the plants.
entries.genesis 30:16: When Jacob came in from the field, Leah told him he was hers that night because she had paid for him with the love-fruits. He went to her, and the trade was kept.
entries.genesis 30:17: God listened to Leah, and she became pregnant and had a fifth son. God noticed her and answered her.
entries.genesis 30:18: Leah named the boy Issachar, saying God had paid her back for giving her servant to her husband. She read the birth as God rewarding her.
entries.genesis 30:19: Leah became pregnant again and had a sixth son. Her family continued to grow.
entries.genesis 30:20: Leah named him Zebulun, saying God had given her a good gift and now her husband would live with her because she had six sons. She hoped the children would earn her Jacob's love.
entries.genesis 30:21: Afterward Leah had a daughter and named her Dinah. The account notes this daughter among her children.
entries.genesis 30:22: Then God remembered Rachel, heard her prayer, and made her able to have children. After years of waiting, God acted on her behalf.
entries.genesis 30:23: Rachel became pregnant and had a son, saying God had taken away her shame. In that culture, childlessness was felt as disgrace, and she saw it lifted.
entries.genesis 30:24: She named him Joseph and prayed that the Lord would give her another son. Her name for him carried hope for more.
entries.genesis 30:25: After Joseph was born, Jacob told Laban he wanted to leave and go back to his own homeland. He was ready to move on after years of service.
entries.genesis 30:26: Jacob asked for his wives and children, for whom he had worked for Laban, and said Laban knew how hard he had worked. He wanted to leave with the family he had earned.
entries.genesis 30:27: Laban urged Jacob to stay, saying he had learned from signs that the Lord had blessed him because of Jacob. He knew Jacob's presence had brought him good.
entries.genesis 30:28: Laban told Jacob to name his own wages and he would pay them. He was willing to negotiate to keep Jacob working for him.
entries.genesis 30:29: Jacob reminded Laban that he had seen how well the animals had done under his care. He pointed to the results of his hard work.
entries.genesis 30:30: Jacob said Laban had little before he came and now had much, and the Lord had blessed everything Jacob did, yet Jacob had nothing for his own family. He was asking when he would finally provide for his own household.
entries.genesis 30:31: Laban asked what he should give, and Jacob said he wanted nothing except to keep caring for the flock under one condition. He proposed a different kind of payment.
entries.genesis 30:32: Jacob asked to go through the flock that day and take the spotted, marked, and black sheep and the marked goats as his wages. He set the terms of his pay.
entries.genesis 30:33: Jacob said his honesty could be checked later: any goat or sheep in his flock that did not match the agreed markings could be treated as stolen. He offered a way to prove he was fair.
entries.genesis 30:34: Laban agreed to Jacob's terms. The deal was settled.
entries.genesis 30:35: That same day Laban removed all the marked and colored goats and the black sheep and put them in the care of his sons. He took out the animals Jacob had asked for.
entries.genesis 30:36: Laban sent those animals three days' journey away and left Jacob to care for the rest of the flock. He made sure the agreed animals were far from Jacob.
entries.genesis 30:37: Jacob cut branches from trees and peeled back the bark so white stripes showed on the wood. He was trying a method with the animals.
entries.genesis 30:38: He placed the striped sticks in the watering places where the flock came to drink and mate. He hoped the sight would affect the young born to the flock.
entries.genesis 30:39: The flock gave birth to young that were striped and marked with color. The account reports that the animals came out marked.
entries.genesis 30:40: Jacob kept those marked lambs separate and put his own flock apart from Laban's. He was building up his own animals as the deal allowed.
entries.genesis 30:41: Jacob placed the striped sticks where the strongest animals mated, believing this would make their young come out spotted or streaked. It shows him using a clever breeding strategy to build his own herd.
entries.genesis 30:42: He left the sticks out when the weaker animals mated, so the weak offspring went to Laban and the strong ones to Jacob. In plain terms, he made sure the best animals ended up as his.
entries.genesis 30:43: Jacob became very rich, owning large flocks as well as servants, camels, and donkeys. The point for the reader is that his wealth grew enormously during his time with Laban.
entries.genesis 31:1: Jacob heard Laban's sons saying he had taken their father's wealth for himself. It shows how suspicion was building against Jacob in the family he had served.
entries.genesis 31:2: Jacob noticed that Laban no longer looked at him the same way as before. The relationship had clearly turned cold, which was a warning sign for Jacob.
entries.genesis 31:3: God told Jacob to return to his homeland and promised to be with him. It means God was directing Jacob's next step and would not abandon him on the journey.
entries.genesis 31:4: Jacob called Rachel and Leah out to the field where his flocks were. He chose a private place to talk with his wives about what was happening.
entries.genesis 31:5: Jacob told his wives that their father's attitude toward him had changed, but God had still been with him. It reminds the reader that God's presence can hold steady even when people turn against you.
entries.genesis 31:6: Jacob reminded his wives that he had worked as hard as he could for their father. He wanted them to know he had done his part honestly.
entries.genesis 31:7: Jacob said Laban had cheated him by changing his wages ten times, but God had stopped Laban from harming him. It shows God can protect someone even when others act unfairly.
entries.genesis 31:8: Jacob explained that whatever Laban set as the payment, the flocks produced young that matched it, so Jacob kept gaining. It shows how God kept turning Laban's schemes in Jacob's favor.
entries.genesis 31:9: Jacob said God had taken the livestock from Laban and given it to him. He saw his growing wealth as God's doing, not his own trickery.
entries.genesis 31:10: Jacob described a dream during the mating season in which the male goats were streaked, speckled, and spotted. It was the moment God showed him what was happening with the flocks.
entries.genesis 31:11: In the dream an angel of God called Jacob by name, and Jacob answered that he was listening. It shows Jacob responding to God's direct call.
entries.genesis 31:12: The angel told Jacob to notice the streaked and spotted male goats, because God had seen how Laban had treated him. It means God was aware of the unfairness Jacob had suffered.
entries.genesis 31:13: God identified himself as the God of Bethel, where Jacob had anointed a pillar and made a vow, and told him to leave and return to his birthplace. It reminds the reader that God remembers promises and calls people to move when the time is right.
entries.genesis 31:14: Rachel and Leah answered that they had no share or inheritance left in their father's house. They were saying they had nothing to gain by staying.
entries.genesis 31:15: They said their father treated them like foreigners, sold them, and used up the money. It shows they felt their father had used them for his own benefit.
entries.genesis 31:16: They agreed that the wealth God had taken from their father belonged to them and their children, and they told Jacob to do whatever God had said. It shows them supporting Jacob's obedience to God.
entries.genesis 31:17: Jacob put his wives and sons on camels to get ready to travel. It marks the practical start of the family's journey away from Laban.
entries.genesis 31:18: Jacob sent all his livestock and property ahead of him and set out to return to Isaac in Canaan. He was leaving with everything he had gained in Paddan-aram.
entries.genesis 31:19: While Laban was away shearing sheep, Rachel secretly took her father's household gods. It shows Rachel taking something that did not belong to her, which would later cause trouble.
entries.genesis 31:20: Jacob left without telling Laban, slipping away quietly. He avoided a confrontation, but it also meant Laban was caught off guard.
entries.genesis 31:21: Jacob crossed the Euphrates River with everything he owned and headed toward the hill country of Gilead. He was putting real distance between himself and Laban.
entries.genesis 31:22: Three days later Laban learned that Jacob had run away. The delay gave Jacob a head start on his journey.
entries.genesis 31:23: Laban took his relatives with him, chased Jacob for seven days, and caught up with him in Gilead. It shows Laban was determined to confront Jacob.
entries.genesis 31:24: God came to Laban in a dream at night and warned him not to say anything good or bad to Jacob. It means God was stepping in to protect Jacob from Laban's anger.
entries.genesis 31:25: Laban caught up with Jacob, who had set up his tent in the hill country, and Laban and his relatives camped nearby. The two sides were now face to face.
entries.genesis 31:26: Laban asked Jacob why he had sneaked away and taken his daughters like captives in war. He was accusing Jacob of treating his family dishonorably.
entries.genesis 31:27: Laban complained that Jacob hid his departure instead of leaving openly with joy, singing, and music. He wanted to look like a generous father sending his daughters off properly.
entries.genesis 31:28: Laban said Jacob did not even let him kiss his sons and daughters goodbye, calling it a foolish thing to do. He was expressing hurt and anger at being denied a farewell.
entries.genesis 31:29: Laban admitted he had the power to hurt Jacob, but God had warned him the night before not to speak against Jacob. It shows God's protection was real and effective.
entries.genesis 31:30: Laban said he understood Jacob wanted to go home, but he demanded to know why his gods had been stolen. The missing idols became the main accusation against Jacob.
entries.genesis 31:31: Jacob answered that he was afraid Laban would take his daughters away by force. He explained his secret departure as fear, not malice.
entries.genesis 31:32: Jacob said whoever had the gods should be put to death, and he let Laban search everything, not knowing Rachel had taken them. It shows Jacob was confident but unaware of the danger his own words created.
entries.genesis 31:33: Laban searched Jacob's tent, Leah's tent, and the servants' tents but found nothing, then went into Rachel's tent. The search was thorough but still came up empty.
entries.genesis 31:34: Rachel had hidden the idols in a camel's saddlebag and was sitting on them, so Laban's search missed them. It shows the idols were concealed right under his nose.
entries.genesis 31:35: Rachel told her father she could not stand up because she was having her monthly period, so he did not find the idols. Her excuse kept the theft hidden, though it was a deception.
entries.genesis 31:36: Jacob became angry and challenged Laban, asking what crime he had committed to deserve such a hot pursuit. Jacob felt he was being treated as a criminal without cause.
entries.genesis 31:37: Jacob invited Laban to show anything of his found among Jacob's goods and to lay it out before both families as judges. He wanted the matter settled openly and fairly.
entries.genesis 31:38: Jacob said he had been with Laban for twenty years, and during that time the flocks had not miscarried and he had not eaten any of Laban's rams. He was pointing to his long record of faithful service.
entries.genesis 31:39: Jacob said he did not bring animals torn by wild beasts to Laban but covered the loss himself, and he bore the cost when things were stolen day or night. It shows how much responsibility Jacob carried for Laban's flock.
entries.genesis 31:40: Jacob described his hard life: scorched by heat in the day, freezing at night, and often unable to sleep. It shows the physical cost of his twenty years of work.
entries.genesis 31:41: Jacob sums up twenty hard years of work for Laban, during which his wages were unfairly changed ten times. It shows how long and unfairly he was treated, and reminds the reader that God sees unfair treatment even when no one else does.
entries.genesis 31:42: Jacob says that if God had not been with him, Laban would have sent him away empty-handed. God saw his hard work and hardship and defended him, which encourages the reader that God notices their struggles too.
entries.genesis 31:43: Laban claims everything Jacob has as his own, yet he asks what he can do for his daughters and grandchildren. He is unwilling to admit wrongdoing but still wants to keep a connection with his family.
entries.genesis 31:44: Laban proposes a formal agreement between himself and Jacob to settle their dispute. It shows that making a clear, agreed boundary can end a conflict fairly.
entries.genesis 31:45: Jacob sets up a single stone as a marker for the agreement. It is a simple, lasting sign that something important has been settled.
entries.genesis 31:46: Jacob has his men gather stones into a pile, and then everyone shares a meal beside it. Sharing food together seals the peace between them in an ordinary, human way.
entries.genesis 31:47: Laban names the stone pile in his own language and Jacob names it in his, both meaning the same thing. Each man marks the agreement in his own tongue, showing it belongs to both of them.
entries.genesis 31:48: Laban explains that the stones stand as a witness to the agreement between him and Jacob. The pile is a visible reminder of the promise both men have made.
entries.genesis 31:49: The place is also called Mizpah, meaning a watchtower, because Laban asks the Lord to watch over them when they are apart. It reminds the reader that God sees what happens even when people are separated.
entries.genesis 31:50: Laban warns Jacob not to mistreat his daughters or take other wives, and says God will witness it even if no person sees. It teaches that God sees hidden wrongs, so people should treat others rightly even when unobserved.
entries.genesis 31:51: Laban points out the stones and the pillar he has set between himself and Jacob. These objects are meant to be a clear, visible reminder of their agreement.
entries.genesis 31:52: The stones mark a boundary: neither man will cross over to harm the other. It sets a limit that keeps the peace between them.
entries.genesis 31:53: Laban calls on the God of their ancestors to judge between them, and Jacob swears by the God his father Isaac feared. Both men appeal to God as the one who will hold them to their promise.
entries.genesis 31:54: Jacob offers a sacrifice on the mountain and then everyone eats and rests there. The agreement is sealed with worship and a shared meal, ending the dispute on a peaceful note.
entries.genesis 31:55: Early the next morning Laban kisses and blesses his daughters and returns home. The conflict ends with a farewell rather than a fight, and the family parts in peace.
entries.genesis 32:1: Jacob was traveling and suddenly met angels sent by God. It shows God was watching over him on his journey, and he still watches over us.
entries.genesis 32:2: Seeing the angels, Jacob called the place 'God's army,' because they looked like a great camp of soldiers. God's protection is real even when we feel weak.
entries.genesis 32:3: Jacob sent messengers ahead to his brother Esau in the region of Edom. He was trying to make contact carefully before meeting him.
entries.genesis 32:4: Jacob told the messengers to greet Esau humbly and explain that he had been staying with Laban all this time. He wanted to approach his brother gently.
entries.genesis 32:5: Jacob listed his wealth and asked the messengers to tell Esau, hoping to find favor with him. He was trying to smooth things over with gifts and kind words.
entries.genesis 32:6: The messengers returned with alarming news: Esau was coming to meet Jacob with four hundred men. That sounded like an army, so Jacob's fears grew.
entries.genesis 32:7: Jacob was terrified and anxious, so he divided his people and animals into two groups. Fear made him plan for the worst.
entries.genesis 32:8: He reasoned that if Esau attacked one group, the other group could escape. It was a practical survival plan born out of fear.
entries.genesis 32:9: Jacob prayed to the God of his grandfather and father, reminding God that He had told him to return home. He turned to God in his fear.
entries.genesis 32:10: Jacob admitted he did not deserve any of God's kindness, recalling that he had crossed the Jordan with only a walking stick and now had become two large camps. He was expressing humble gratitude.
entries.genesis 32:11: Jacob begged God to rescue him from Esau, fearing Esau would kill him and his family. He honestly told God what he was afraid of.
entries.genesis 32:12: Jacob reminded God of His promise to bless him and make his descendants as numerous as the sand. He was holding God to His word.
entries.genesis 32:13: Jacob stayed there overnight and then selected gifts from his possessions to send to Esau. He hoped the gifts would soften his brother's heart.
entries.genesis 32:14: He chose two hundred female goats and twenty male goats, plus two hundred female sheep and twenty male sheep. These were generous gifts meant to please Esau.
entries.genesis 32:15: He also sent thirty camels with their young, forty cows, ten bulls, twenty female donkeys, and ten male donkeys. It was a large and costly gift.
entries.genesis 32:16: Jacob put each herd under separate servants and told them to go ahead of him with space between the herds. The spaced-out gifts would make a big impression.
entries.genesis 32:17: Jacob instructed the servant leading the first herd on what to say if Esau asked who owned them and where they were going. He wanted every answer to point to him.
entries.genesis 32:18: The servant was to tell Esau that the animals belonged to Jacob and were a gift for him, and that Jacob himself was coming behind. Jacob was presenting himself as a humble servant.
entries.genesis 32:19: Jacob gave the same instructions to the second, third, and all the other servants with the herds. Everyone was to give the same message to Esau.
entries.genesis 32:20: They were also to say that Jacob was coming right behind them. Jacob hoped the gifts would calm Esau's anger before they met face to face.
entries.genesis 32:21: So the gift herds went ahead, and Jacob stayed in the camp that night. He was waiting anxiously for the meeting.
entries.genesis 32:22: During the night Jacob got up and took his two wives, two servant-women, and eleven children across the Jabbok River. He was moving his family to safety.
entries.genesis 32:23: He sent them and everything he had across the stream. He made sure his family was safe before facing what came next.
entries.genesis 32:24: Jacob was left alone, and a man wrestled with him until daybreak. This was a mysterious, intense struggle that lasted all night.
entries.genesis 32:25: When the man saw he could not overpower Jacob, he struck Jacob's hip socket and dislocated it. Jacob was left wounded but still holding on.
entries.genesis 32:26: The man asked to be released because dawn was coming, but Jacob refused unless he received a blessing. Jacob would not let go without something from God.
entries.genesis 32:27: The man asked Jacob his name, and Jacob answered. Naming him was part of what was about to change.
entries.genesis 32:28: The man gave Jacob a new name, Israel, because he had struggled with God and with people and had prevailed. His new name marked a new identity and calling.
entries.genesis 32:29: Jacob asked the man's name, but the man refused to tell him and instead blessed him. The blessing was given even though the mystery remained.
entries.genesis 32:30: Jacob named the place Peniel, meaning 'face of God,' because he had seen God face to face and survived. He was amazed that he lived through such a close encounter.
entries.genesis 32:31: As Jacob passed Peniel, the sun rose, and he walked with a limp because of his injured hip. He carried a lasting reminder of that night's struggle.
entries.genesis 32:32: Because of this, the people of Israel have never eaten the muscle at the hip socket of an animal. The custom remembers Jacob's injury that night.
entries.genesis 33:1: Jacob looked up and saw his brother Esau approaching with four hundred men, so he quickly split his family into groups. It shows how afraid Jacob still was, and it reminds us that facing a feared situation often starts with fear before it starts with peace.
entries.genesis 33:2: Jacob arranged the groups so the servant women and their children were closest to danger, with Leah's family next and Rachel and Joseph safest at the back. He was protecting those he loved most, but it also shows favoritism that would later hurt his family.
entries.genesis 33:3: Jacob walked ahead of everyone and bowed low to the ground seven times as he approached his brother. He was showing deep respect and trying to calm Esau, humbling himself before the brother he had wronged.
entries.genesis 33:4: Instead of attacking, Esau ran to Jacob, hugged him, kissed him, and both men cried. The feared meeting turned into forgiveness, showing that reconciliation can be far better than we expect.
entries.genesis 33:5: Esau noticed the women and children and asked who they were, and Jacob answered that they were gifts from God's kindness. Jacob credited God for his family rather than his own cleverness.
entries.genesis 33:6: The servant women and their children came forward and bowed before Esau. They showed respect to the brother Jacob had feared, keeping peace in a tense moment.
entries.genesis 33:7: Leah and her children came and bowed, and last came Joseph and Rachel, doing the same. The whole family honored Esau, completing the respectful greeting Jacob had begun.
entries.genesis 33:8: Esau asked about all the herds Jacob had sent ahead, and Jacob said they were a gift to win his favor. Jacob was still trying to make peace with gifts, unsure whether Esau had truly forgiven him.
entries.genesis 33:9: Esau said he already had plenty and told Jacob to keep his animals. He was refusing the payment, which suggests he was not holding a grudge and wanted no debt between them.
entries.genesis 33:10: Jacob insisted, saying that seeing Esau's friendly face was like seeing God's face, and asked him to accept the gift. He was saying that Esau's forgiveness felt like a gift from God, and he wanted the relationship truly restored.
entries.genesis 33:11: Jacob urged Esau to take the gift, saying God had been good to him and he had enough, and Esau finally accepted. Giving and receiving the gift sealed their peace and showed Jacob's gratitude to God.
entries.genesis 33:12: Esau offered to travel together and go ahead of Jacob. It was a friendly offer, showing he wanted to stay close to his brother.
entries.genesis 33:13: Jacob explained that the children were young and the animals had babies, so moving too fast would kill them. He was being practical and careful, asking Esau to be patient with his slower pace.
entries.genesis 33:14: Jacob asked Esau to go on ahead and said he would follow slowly at the pace his family and animals could handle, until he reached Esau at Seir. It sounded polite, but Jacob may also have been keeping some distance rather than traveling together.
entries.genesis 33:15: Esau offered to leave some of his men with Jacob, but Jacob said there was no need since Esau was pleased with him. Jacob politely declined, perhaps wanting to travel independently.
entries.genesis 33:16: Esau turned back that day and headed home to Seir. The brothers parted peacefully, which was the main thing Jacob had hoped for.
entries.genesis 33:17: Jacob traveled to Succoth, where he built a house and shelters for his animals, and that is how the place got its name. He settled down for a while after the tense meeting with Esau.
entries.genesis 33:18: Jacob arrived safely from Paddan-aram at Shechem in Canaan and set up his tents near the town. God had brought him safely back to the land promised to his family.
entries.genesis 33:19: Jacob bought the field where he camped from the sons of Hamor for a hundred pieces of money. Buying land showed he intended to stay and put down roots in Canaan.
entries.genesis 33:20: Jacob built an altar there and named it El, the God of Israel, meaning God is the God of Israel. He was marking the place as a place of worship and declaring that God had been faithful to him.
entries.genesis 34:1: Dinah, Jacob's daughter, went out to visit the local women. It shows she was just being social, and nothing she did caused what happened next.
entries.genesis 34:2: Shechem, a local ruler's son, saw her and forced himself on her. This was a violent assault, not a romance.
entries.genesis 34:3: Afterward Shechem felt strong affection for her and tried to comfort her. Even so, his feelings did not undo the harm he had done.
entries.genesis 34:4: Shechem asked his father to arrange a marriage with Dinah. He wanted to keep her, but that did not make right what he had already done.
entries.genesis 34:5: Jacob heard what had happened but stayed quiet until his sons came home from the fields. He held back instead of acting right away.
entries.genesis 34:6: Hamor, Shechem's father, came to talk with Jacob about the situation. He came to negotiate rather than to apologize for the wrong.
entries.genesis 34:7: Jacob's sons came in and were furious at the outrage done to their sister. They saw it as a terrible wrong that should never have happened.
entries.genesis 34:8: Hamor asked them to let his son marry Dinah, saying the young man deeply wanted her. He treated the assault as a matter of arranging a marriage.
entries.genesis 34:9: Hamor proposed that the two families intermarry and become one people. He was offering a partnership between the groups.
entries.genesis 34:10: He invited Jacob's family to settle in the land, trade, and own property. It was a generous offer, but it ignored the wrong that had been done.
entries.genesis 34:11: Shechem spoke to Dinah's father and brothers, promising to pay whatever they asked. He was trying to buy his way to having her.
entries.genesis 34:12: He said he would pay any bride-price they named, however high, if only he could marry her. He thought money could settle the matter.
entries.genesis 34:13: Jacob's sons answered Shechem and his father with a lie because of what had been done to their sister. Their anger led them to deceive.
entries.genesis 34:14: They said they could not give their sister to a man who was not circumcised, calling it a disgrace. They used a religious custom as a cover for their plan.
entries.genesis 34:15: They said they would agree only if every male among them was circumcised like them. This was a trick, not a real condition for peace.
entries.genesis 34:16: They promised to intermarry and live as one people if the men agreed. It sounded like a fair deal, but they did not mean it.
entries.genesis 34:17: They warned that if the men refused, they would take their sister and leave. This gave their demand a false sense of firmness.
entries.genesis 34:18: Hamor and his son Shechem liked what they heard. They accepted the offer without suspecting the trap.
entries.genesis 34:19: Shechem acted quickly because he was delighted with Dinah, and he was the most honored man in his father's house. His status made the whole town more willing to go along.
entries.genesis 34:20: Hamor and Shechem went to the town gate, where business was done, and spoke to the men. They presented the plan to the whole community.
entries.genesis 34:21: They told the townsmen that Jacob's family wanted peace and should be allowed to live and trade there, and that the two groups should intermarry. They made the plan sound good for everyone.
entries.genesis 34:22: They explained that the only condition was that all their males be circumcised. The townsmen were told this was the price of the agreement.
entries.genesis 34:23: They pointed out that Jacob's livestock and wealth would then become theirs, so they urged the men to agree. Greed helped win the town over.
entries.genesis 34:24: All the men of the town listened to Hamor and Shechem and were circumcised. The whole male population went along with the plan.
entries.genesis 34:25: On the third day, while the men were still sore, Simeon and Levi, Dinah's brothers, attacked the town with swords and killed every male. They used the men's weakened condition to carry out a massacre.
entries.genesis 34:26: They also killed Hamor and his son Shechem, then took Dinah from Shechem's house and left. They rescued their sister, but through great violence.
entries.genesis 34:27: The other sons of Jacob came and plundered the wounded town because of what had been done to their sister. They turned the whole town into a target.
entries.genesis 34:28: They seized the flocks, herds, donkeys, and everything in the town and fields. They took all the town's livestock and property.
entries.genesis 34:29: They carried off all the wealth, the children, and the wives, and looted everything in the houses. The whole community suffered for one man's crime.
entries.genesis 34:30: Jacob told Simeon and Levi that they had brought trouble on him and made him hated by the local peoples, who would now attack his small family. He feared the violence would destroy them all.
entries.genesis 34:31: Simeon and Levi answered that they could not let their sister be treated like a prostitute. They defended their revenge as standing up for her honor.
entries.genesis 35:1: God tells Jacob to go back to Bethel and settle there, and to build an altar to the God who helped him when he was running from his brother. It reminds the reader that God calls us to remember and honor the times he has rescued us.
entries.genesis 35:2: Jacob tells everyone in his household to get rid of their foreign gods, wash up, and change their clothes. It means the reader should clear out anything that competes with God and start fresh before worshiping him.
entries.genesis 35:3: Jacob explains they are going to Bethel to build an altar to God, who answered him in his trouble and stayed with him everywhere he went. It encourages the reader to trust that God is present through hard times and travels.
entries.genesis 35:4: The people hand over their foreign gods and earrings, and Jacob buries them under a tree at Shechem. It shows the reader that getting rid of idols should be done decisively, not kept around as a backup.
entries.genesis 35:5: As they travel, a fear of God falls on the surrounding towns, so no one attacks Jacob's family. It means God can protect his people in ways they never could arrange themselves.
entries.genesis 35:6: Jacob and all his people arrive at Luz, also called Bethel, in Canaan. It simply marks the family reaching the place God had told them to go.
entries.genesis 35:7: Jacob builds an altar there and names the place El-bethel, because God had appeared to him there when he was fleeing from his brother. It shows the reader that remembering where God met you builds gratitude and faith.
entries.genesis 35:8: Deborah, Rebekah's old nurse, dies and is buried under a tree near Bethel, which they name Allon-bacuth, meaning the oak of weeping. It reminds the reader that grief is real and worth honoring, even in the middle of God's work.
entries.genesis 35:9: After Jacob returns from Paddan-aram, God appears to him again and blesses him. It shows the reader that God keeps showing up in a person's life, not just once.
entries.genesis 35:10: God tells Jacob his name will no longer be Jacob but Israel, and that becomes his name. It means God gives people a new identity that reflects who they are becoming, not just who they were.
entries.genesis 35:11: God calls himself God Almighty and tells Jacob to be fruitful and multiply, promising nations and kings will come from him. It reassures the reader that God's promises are big and carry forward to future generations.
entries.genesis 35:12: God promises to give Jacob and his descendants the same land he gave Abraham and Isaac. It shows the reader that God keeps promises made long ago, even across generations.
entries.genesis 35:13: God then leaves the place where he had been speaking with Jacob. It simply marks the end of this face-to-face encounter.
entries.genesis 35:14: Jacob sets up a stone pillar where God spoke with him and pours a drink offering and oil on it. It shows the reader that responding to God with worship and remembrance is a fitting reply to his presence.
entries.genesis 35:15: Jacob names the place Bethel, meaning house of God, because God had spoken with him there. It reminds the reader to mark and remember the places where God has met them.
entries.genesis 35:16: As they travel on from Bethel, Rachel goes into hard labor before they reach Ephrath. It shows the reader that life's journeys include painful, unexpected moments.
entries.genesis 35:17: When the pain is worst, the midwife tells Rachel not to fear because she is having another son. It means even in agony there can be news of hope.
entries.genesis 35:18: Rachel dies giving birth and names the baby Ben-oni, but Jacob renames him Benjamin. It shows the reader that a father's love can turn a name of sorrow into one of strength.
entries.genesis 35:19: Rachel dies and is buried beside the road to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. It marks a real loss in the family's story and the place where it happened.
entries.genesis 35:20: Jacob sets up a pillar over Rachel's grave, and it is still called Rachel's tomb. It shows the reader that remembering loved ones with lasting markers is a way of honoring them.
entries.genesis 35:21: Israel travels on and sets up camp beyond the tower of the flock. It simply continues the family's journey.
entries.genesis 35:22: While living there, Reuben sleeps with Bilhah, his father's concubine, and Israel hears about it. It shows the reader that sin inside a family causes deep damage, even when it is kept quiet.
entries.genesis 35:23: This lists Jacob's twelve sons, starting with Leah's six: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, and Zebulun. It shows the reader how God's promise of a nation was taking shape through an ordinary family.
entries.genesis 35:24: Rachel's two sons are Joseph and Benjamin. It continues the list of Jacob's twelve sons.
entries.genesis 35:25: Bilhah, Rachel's servant, has two sons: Dan and Naphtali. It shows the reader that God's plan included every branch of this complicated family.
entries.genesis 35:26: Zilpah, Leah's servant, has two sons, Gad and Asher, and these are all the sons Jacob had in Paddan-aram. It completes the count of the twelve sons.
entries.genesis 35:27: Jacob finally comes to his father Isaac at Mamre, also called Kiriath-arba or Hebron, where Abraham and Isaac had lived. It shows the reader that long journeys and family reunions are part of God's bigger story.
entries.genesis 35:28: Isaac lives to be 180 years old. It simply records the length of his life.
entries.genesis 35:29: Isaac dies at a good old age and is buried by his sons Jacob and Esau. It shows the reader that a long life ends in peace, and that even estranged brothers can come together to honor their father.
